newsitem.title: USA: Hearings have theatrical touches but little drama.
newsitem.headline: Hearings have theatrical touches but little drama.

text.p: It had all the trappings of a Broadway premiere: a bright stage, characters ranging from Buddhist monks to White House aides, not one, but two surprise opening speeches and paparazzi lined up hours before the show.
But whether the Senate Government Affairs Committee's hearings into campaign finance abuses, which began Tuesday, will actually produce any real drama remains to be seen.

Sen. Fred Thompson, the Tennessee Republican who chairs the committee, did his best to enliven the proceedings by making a surprise opening soliloquy alleging China sought to buy its way into U.S. politics last year.

Sen. John Glenn, the Ohio Democrat who is the committee's ranking minority member, also pulled a rabbit out of his hat, announcing that John Huang, a one-time Commerce Department official turned Democratic party fund-raiser, had offered to testify before the committee if given limited immunity.

But the 16 opening statements that took up the committee's first four-hour session were often dull, repetitive and self-serving, with some senators admitting there is little, if any, chance the hearings will produce campaign finance reform.

And although many senators evoked Watergate, Tuesday's session appeared a far cry from the nearly quarter-century old political scandal in which congressional hearings helped drive President Richard Nixon to resignation.

Thompson, who wanted to hold the campaign finance hearings in the old room where the Watergate hearings took place, instead chose a spacious room in a modern Senate office building wired for television lights, sound and cameras.

The main excitement at Tuesday's hearing, packed with more than 100 journalists and photographers, was the news that Huang, a former mid-level political appointee at the Commerce Department who became a Democratic fund-raiser, might testify.

Huang told the committee through his lawyer he was ready to testify if given immunity from any criminal charges except espionage, disclosing classified information, acting as a foreign agent, perjury or making false statements under oath.

Huang, who previously insisted that he would exercise his fifth amendment right against self-incrimination, raised $1.6 million that the Democratic National Committee has since given back, saying the money came from questionable sources.
The committee directed its lawyers to examine exactly what the former official might be willing to say under oath before deciding whether to accept his offer.

And Sen. Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said the committee should first move ahead with testimony from others, including Buddhist nuns and monks who attended a controversial fund-raiser with Vice President Al Gore in a Buddhist temple.

The committee is also after bigger game and has subpoenaed Harold Ickes, Clinton's deputy chief of staff and de facto campaign chairman last year; Don Fowler, the DNC's former co-chairman, and Clinton confidant Bruce Lindsey.
